How can I achieve lower CV and have smaller confidence intervals?

Sorry for this basic question. Any insights would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Carolina

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian,

I'm afraid I don't have a recipe to use the coverage as a raster layer, but I do have a small piece of advice that might help a bit.  The coverage probabilities are stored in the Distance project's Data File, which is always called DistData.mdb and lives in the Data Folder of the project (same place as the shapefiles).  If you open that file in Microsoft Access (don't upgrade the format, by the way), you'll see a table for each Data Layer in the project; if you look in the table associated with the coverage grid, you'll find a field that corresponds with each field for which a coverage has been generated.  There is also an ID field, which allows you to link the records to those in the shapefile (which has a LinkID field).  You can find out more about the format of the Data File in the help file "Appendix - Inside Distance", "Data File Reference".  Hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon list,

After I emailed, I exchanged different emails with Eric Rexstad, thanks once again Eric. Here a summary of what he recommended, in case this could be of insight for some of you:

The patterns I first reported resulted from analysis done with all species pooled. Recognizing that all species have different detection functions, my results  were influenced by this.

Bottom-line: If you have more than one study area, focus on species and site-specific differences rather than trying to make sense of the overall pooled data.

Sincerely,

Carolina

You could simply note that the patterns you had first reported had been for all species and all sites pooled.  That upon further analysis the patterns in the analysis became more clear.

messages.subject_clean: mrds Full independence with binned data
messages.body_plain:
I just discovered a bug in mrds with the AIC calculation for binned data under full independence. Under full independence the distance data are not used in the fitting but the code produces a log-likelihood value for the ds portion using the conditional detection functions.  Prior to version 2.1.1 the code was using the unbinned distances in that calculation which was approximate but not strictly correct especially with a few bins. That was changed in v2.1.1 but as it turns out there was a bug in the code which was producing incorrect values.  It has been fixed on github and we will release a version on CRAN at some point. In the meantime if you need a patched version contact me. Sorry for any inconvenience.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Detection probability equals to one
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I used Distance 6.2 to analyse my bird point count data. For some species, the models with the best support according to AIC estimate the detection probability as 1.0. I find these results surprising assuming that the detection probability should be always lower than one in real world.

I collected the data in two distance intervals (0-30 m and 30-100 m). Number of records of each species of concern in the study area ranged between 40 and 100. For each species I applied four recommended models (uniform key with cosine adjustments; half-normal key with cosine adjustments; half-normal key with Hermite polynomial adjustments; hazard-rate key with simple polynomial adjustments). Hazard-rate model seems nonsensical (huge density estimate, no AIC, warning about “No fit possible”), other models fit data very similarly. Both half-normal models have the same AIC and uniform model has AIC of one to two smaller.

The main problem is that the detection probability (p) is often (always when using the uniform model) equal or very close to one. I think that this is an unreasonable result, but I do not know what's wrong. Given that the model with p = 1 have often the lowest AIC (or ranks similar to other models), it is difficult to find objective reasons to reject it and use the alternative ones with p less than 1. I would be happy if some of you could provide me some advice on how to solve this problem. I attach exported detection probability plot and results of uniform key with cosine adjustments model.

Moreover, MCDS engine always generate some warning messages.

For half normal models:

** Warning: The number of intervals - 1 equals the number of key parameters 1 so no adjustments can be made. **

For uniform model:

** Warning: The number of adjustment parameters allowed has been reduced to 1 because of limited number of intervals. **

and for some species also:

** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **

Please, could you help me to fix these issues?

All the best

Ondřej Bušek

messages.subject_clean: Automating density estimation for multiple species using the 'distance' package in R
messages.body_plain:
This post is somewhat similar to one from Jan 2013: 'Estimating Density for multiple species in multiple strata' where I have multiple species that I need to get density estimates for, which is time consuming, and would like to automate this somehow in R.

To give you an idea of my data, I am working with line transect bird data collected from 2011-2013 over large spatial scales in the Australian Outback (sparse vegetation so birds can be seen/heard from far distances). The same 150 census stops are surveyed once a year, with 50 census stops spaced evenly along each of three 800km megatransects. At each census stop, a series of eight (non-independent) 400m line transects are conducted. I want to get density estimates for each species in each year. I have been doing this in program distance by estimating density at the census stop-level (so ~150 density estimates per year) so that I can see how a species' density is changing at the same census stop over subsequent years. I use a global detection function resolution so that I have enough observations for a species to fit a reliable detection function (60 obs is recommended for line transects).

I suspect automating density estimates in R will be difficult because what I have been doing in program distance is fairly manually intensive. Firstly, I find that using the recommended 5% truncation for line transects still leaves a long 'tail' at the end of the detection probability plot (possibly because birds are able to be detected at very far distances in this survey), so I usually end up eyeballing where a 15% detection probability (recommended in Buckland 2001) hits the detection function line and use this as a baseline truncation distance. Secondly, distances were often estimated in the field by rounding to the nearest 10m interval (causing spikes at 10m, 20m, 30m, etc), thus heaping occurs, so I have been correcting for this by manually binning intervals in the Data Filter, with bin width gradually widening with increasing distance from 0 (e.g. 5m, 15m, 25m, 35m, 55m, 75m, 105m etc.). The width and number of intervals that I choose can depend on how species are detected (e.g. visually or aurally) or species' identity (e.g. raptors usually require fewer and much wider bins that go to farther distances since these species are able to be detected at much larger scales). What makes it equally time consuming is there is no one metric that tells you which model fits the best detection function (AIC vs chi-square GOF vs eye-balling how well the detection fxn fits the data + %CV) so I usually run a few different models with different binning/truncation combinations until I find a good balance of these metrics. (If any of these steps are incorrect or can be done more efficiently please let me know!)

If there is a way to automate these processes in R for each species, I would love to know as this would save me heaps of time now and in the future. Thanks!

Cheers,
Michelle Gibson
--
Michelle Gibson
PhD student
School of Biological and Biomedical Sciences
Durham University
United Kingdom

Hi Michelle & list members,

This seems like a very time consuming process, so I can see why you'd
want to automate the process.

I have a few suggestions that might help you out here:

1. Make your process uniform -- if you come up with a set of decision
rules (and an ordering for them!) for selecting a detection function,
you can at least know the way in which your model is optimal, rather
than having different models selected because of different metrics. This
makes retracing your steps easier and your research more easily
reproducible.

2. Automate -- using the plyr package one can take "slices" through a
data set in R and run models on the subsets. This poster from ISEC 2014
may be useful: http://dill.github.io/posters/Rexstad-ISEC2014.pdf In
particular the bottom middle panel shows a simple example of using the
dlply function from plyr to run multiple analyses. This article may also
be useful: http://www.jstatsoft.org/v40/i01

3. Think of an automated process as a "first cut" -- if you're not happy
with the resulting models and do need to manually review them, then try
this after doing some automation. Automation should at least reduce the
number of steps you have to carry out manually.

I hope this helps!

best,
--dave

Ana, I’m assuming you ticked the box to indicate that these were factor-type covariates.  Not sure what you mean when you say that Distance only recognises one level.  You should only get one parameter estimate for each of habitat and season.  When you have 2 levels of a factor, you have just one parameter to estimate the difference between them.  So Distance essentially fits a detection function assuming one level, then gives you a parameter estimate telling you how the scale parameter of the detection function changes for the other level.  But you should get a plot of the estimated detection function for each habitat type and for each season.

Steve Buckland

> This post is somewhat similar to one from Jan 2013: 'Estimating Density for multiple species in multiple strata' where I have multiple species that I need to get density estimates for, which is time consuming, and would like to automate this somehow in R.
>
> To give you an idea of my data, I am working with line transect bird data collected from 2011-2013 over large spatial scales in the Australian Outback (sparse vegetation so birds can be seen/heard from far distances). The same 150 census stops are surveyed once a year, with 50 census stops spaced evenly along each of three 800km megatransects. At each census stop, a series of eight (non-independent) 400m line transects are conducted. I want to get density estimates for each species in each year. I have been doing this in program distance by estimating density at the census stop-level (so ~150 density estimates per year) so that I can see how a species' density is changing at the same census stop over subsequent years. I use a global detection function resolution so that I have enough observations for a species to fit a reliable detection function (60 obs is recommended for line transects).
>
> I suspect automating density estimates in R will be difficult because what I have been doing in program distance is fairly manually intensive. Firstly, I find that using the recommended 5% truncation for line transects still leaves a long 'tail' at the end of the detection probability plot (possibly because birds are able to be detected at very far distances in this survey), so I usually end up eyeballing where a 15% detection probability (recommended in Buckland 2001) hits the detection function line and use this as a baseline truncation distance. Secondly, distances were often estimated in the field by rounding to the nearest 10m interval (causing spikes at 10m, 20m, 30m, etc), thus heaping occurs, so I have been correcting for this by manually binning intervals in the Data Filter, with bin width gradually widening with increasing distance from 0 (e.g. 5m, 15m, 25m, 35m, 55m, 75m, 105m etc.). The width and number of intervals that I choose can depend on how species are detected (e.g. visually or aurally) or species' identity (e.g. raptors usually require fewer and much wider bins that go to farther distances since these species are able to be detected at much larger scales). What makes it equally time consuming is there is no one metric that tells you which model fits the best detection function (AIC vs chi-square GOF vs eye-balling how well the detection fxn fits the data + %CV) so I usually run a few different models with different binning/truncation combinations until I find a good balance of these metrics. (If any of these steps are incorrect or can be done more efficiently please let me know!)
>
> If there is a way to automate these processes in R for each species, I would love to know as this would save me heaps of time now and in the future. Thanks!
>
> Cheers,
> Michelle Gibson
> --

> School of Biological and Biomedical Sciences
> Durham University
> United Kingdom

Regarding goodness of fit from ds() in R; consider using the KS-test or the CVM-test for assessing goodness of fit.  These do not require binning of exact distance data as does the chi-square test.

If you look at the vignette on the distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org> website (http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html) you can see where a goodness of fit has been conducted and the CVM test statistics and P-values are extracted and placed onto the plot:

covar.fit <- ddf.gof(whale.strat.covariate$ddf)
message <- paste("Cramer von-Mises W=", round(covar.fit$dsgof$CvM$W,3),
                 "\nP=", round(covar.fit$dsgof$CvM$p,3))
text(0.6, 0.1, message, cex=0.8)

messages.subject: CV plotting issues in dsm [R]
messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk (who use dsm in R),

Adrian Schiavini e-mailed me earlier today with a bug when plotting CV
results in dsm (i.e. in plot.dsm.var). Resulting plots looked odd and
the following warnings were printed:

Warning messages:
    1: In Ops.factor(width, 2) : / not meaningful for factors
    2: In Ops.factor(width, 2) : / not meaningful for factors
    3: In Ops.factor(height, 2) : / not meaningful for factors
    4: In Ops.factor(height, 2) : / not meaningful for factors

This is due to a bug in the plotting code where I coerced a list of
data.frames in a data.frame using matrix(). Unfortunately, I had
forgotten that matrix() will simplify so that all of it's arguments are
of the same type (see "Combining data frames" in
http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Data-structures.html for an explanation if you're
interested).

In any case, the version of dsm on github has now been patched. You can
install this using devtools:

install.packages("devtools")
library("devtools")
install_github("DistanceDevelopment/dsm")

cheers,
--dave
